title: The old rehatnamas
hookLine: earlier codes differ in detail; the 1950 code is the shared reference

cards: Two recipe cards for the same dish. One in a grandmother's hand, splattered, with a note in the margin. One printed in a community cookbook, neat and measured.
One says a handful and the other says a cup, and one adds a spice the other never mentions. Which is right? Families have that argument at holiday tables.
Sikhs have a version of it too, written down over generations. Before the shared code this path has been reading, there were older ones, and they don't all say the same thing.

teach.h: A REHATNAMA: A WRITING ON REHAT.
teach.b: A rehatnama is a writing about rehat, the Sikh way of living. In the generations after the Tenth Guru, Sikhs wrote several. Some carry the names of people tradition places near the Guru, such as the poet Bhai Nand Lal.
They set out how a Sikh should rise, pray, dress, eat and treat others.
Side by side, they share a lot of ground: remember the Name, keep the hair, live honestly, share. Read closely, they differ. One stresses a rule another leaves out.
Some carry the worries and the language of their own time and place. Who wrote which parts, and when, is still discussed.
So, much later, Sikh bodies worked together to agree on one shared code, the Sikh Rehat Maryada, published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee; you met its writing earlier on this path.
Today it's the shared reference gurdwaras point to, though some groups and some historic places keep customs of their own beside it. Here's the turn.

teach.h: EVERY CODE MEASURED BY THE GRANTH.
teach.b: A code is the community's best written understanding of how to live the Guru's way, and its wording can change from one era to the next.
The Guru it follows does not. The Guru Granth Sahib is fixed, word for word, and every code, old or new, is measured against it, never the other way round.

how: Sikh scholars study the older rehatnamas alongside the Sikh Rehat Maryada, which serves as the shared reference for Sikh conduct today.

practice: Bring to mind one rule you've heard said two ways, your family's version and a book's, or a teacher's and a parent's, and hold them side by side. Notice where they agree and where they differ.
Then rest on what both are trying to protect, the thing underneath the two wordings.
